To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
grip strength of 12-month-old human infants predicts mu rhythm attenuation, which is a neural correlate of action observation.
infants’ grip strength predicts mu attenuation during observation, and the relation between grip strength, mu attenuation during observation and object weight is progressively strong.
infants' grip strength predicts attenuation of the mu rhythm during observation of lifting with differently weighted objects.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of bodily experience in action perception, a key component of the human social brain.
the role of the body in perception and its underlying brain mechanisms, and the development of these mechanisms during infancy.
the role of bodily experience in perception and action.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
infants' grip strength predicts the mu rhythm attenuation during action observation.
infants' grip strength predicts their mu rhythm attenuation during the observation of lifting actions.
infants' grip strength predicts the mu rhythm attenuation during the observation of lifting actions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the body's involvement in perception is not limited to the influence of bodily experience on the shared neural system for action perception and production.
bodily characteristics shape perception by influencing the activation of the neural system supporting action perception, and this relation is particularly evident in early ontogenetic stages.
the body's role extends from perception to action and from action to perception.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the body is involved in perception even in the first year of life.
the body plays a key role in perception, even in infancy.
the body is not just involved in perception but also shapes it.
